An ILS approach means instrument landing approach. It means you are landing strictly based on instruments until you are are at mda.

Mda is minimum decent (or decision) altitude. At which point, if you can't see the runway you are to abort your landing, declare missed approach, and immediately begin your ascent based on published ils procedures. Generally the recommendationn is to proceed to your first alternate airport. Pilots may opt to try again, but so long as you didn't screw up the first approach there generally isn't a point.

There are many types of ils systems. One type has descent guidance. When you are on the the correct descent slope angle, speed, and at the right point in time/distance, you are on the glide slope.

Ils landings are only allowed for instrument rated pilots. This includes instrument rated private pilots (vs vfr), commercial pilots, and military pilots.

Pilot fag here: The glide path is the approach course to the runway. Usually around 3 degrees. An ILS stands for Instrument Landing System. It's a ground-based precision instrument approach that can be done in zero visibility with cloud ceilings as low as 200 feet for most instrument appropriate aircraft, or even down to the runway with aircraft capable of higher category ILSs. It's basically a way to find the runway through clouds using ground radio that gives lateral and vertical guidance.

The only other thing I'd note is that there are non-precision instrument approaches as well that provide only lateral guidance to the plane. Not sure if any of that's significant or not, but worth mentioning.
